title: The Beginning of Wisdom
subtitle: Proverbs 1 — The Fear of the Lord
description: Walk through Proverbs 1 and discover what it truly means to fear the Lord. Explore the Hebrew concept of reverential awe and why Solomon says this is where all knowledge begins.

title: The Minister's Self-Watch
subtitle: From Spurgeon's Lectures to My Students
description: From Spurgeon's Lectures to My Students: the vital importance of watching over your own soul before ministering to others. Woven with Proverbs 4:23 on guarding the heart.

title: The Treasure of Wisdom
subtitle: Proverbs 2 — Seeking Like Silver
description: Proverbs 2 calls us to seek wisdom like hidden treasure. Discover the Puritan approach to deep Scripture study and why active pursuit of God's Word transforms the soul.

title: The Soul Winner's Prayer Life
subtitle: From Spurgeon's The Soul Winner
description: Drawing from Spurgeon's The Soul Winner, explore why prayer is the essential foundation of all evangelism. Connected with Proverbs 3:5-6 on trusting God with our witness.

title: Trust in the Lord
subtitle: Proverbs 3 — Lean Not on Your Own Understanding
description: A deep study of Proverbs 3, especially the beloved verses 5-8. What does it really mean to trust with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding?

title: Guard Your Heart
subtitle: Proverbs 4 — Above All Else
description: Proverbs 4:20-27 commands us to guard our hearts above all else. Practical wisdom for daily Christian living in a world full of distraction and temptation.

title: The Puritan Practice of Daily Prayer
subtitle: A Devotional on the Discipline of Prayer
description: How the Puritans structured their prayer lives with morning and evening devotions. Learn the discipline of prayer from Richard Baxter and other godly saints.

title: Flee from Temptation
subtitle: Proverbs 5 — Guarding Against Sin's Lure
description: Proverbs 5 warns against the allure of temptation. Broader application for all forms of enticement that pull us from God, with practical strategies for vigilance.

title: The Sovereignty of God
subtitle: From A.W. Pink's The Attributes of God
description: From A.W. Pink's The Attributes of God: what does it mean that God is sovereign over all things? How does this truth both humble and deeply comfort the believer?

title: Warnings Against Folly
subtitle: Proverbs 6 — The Sluggard and the Ant
description: Proverbs 6 gives us the sluggard and the ant, the seven things God hates, and warnings against surety. Timeless practical wisdom for everyday diligence.

title: The Holiness of God
subtitle: From A.W. Pink's The Attributes of God
description: From A.W. Pink on God's absolute holiness and purity. What this means for how we approach Him and the connection between His holiness and our sanctification.

title: The Danger of Sin's Allure
subtitle: Proverbs 7 — The Seduction of Folly
description: The vivid picture of temptation in Proverbs 7. How sin always promises pleasure but delivers death, and why wisdom is our shield against deception.

title: Wisdom's Call
subtitle: Proverbs 8 — Wisdom in Creation
description: The beautiful personification of Wisdom calling out in Proverbs 8. Wisdom's role in creation and the joy promised to those who find her and walk in her ways.

title: Scripture Meditation: The Lost Discipline
subtitle: A Devotional on Prayerful Reading
description: How the Puritans meditated on Scripture differently from Eastern practices. The lost art of slow, prayerful reading that transforms the mind and heart.

title: The Fear of the Lord is the Beginning of Wisdom
subtitle: Proverbs 9 — Two Feasts, Two Ways
description: Proverbs 9:10 as the cornerstone. The two feasts of wisdom and folly, and what godly fear looks like in the practical rhythms of daily life.

title: The Mortification of Sin
subtitle: From John Owen
description: John Owen's classic teaching on putting sin to death. "Be killing sin, or sin will be killing you." The role of the Holy Spirit in our daily battle.

title: The Righteous and the Wicked
subtitle: Proverbs 10 — Contrasts in Character
description: The rich contrasts in Proverbs 10 between the righteous and the wicked. Themes of the tongue, diligence, and integrity examined verse by verse.

title: The Art of Divine Contentment
subtitle: From Thomas Watson
description: Thomas Watson's teaching on finding contentment in God alone. How discontentment is a root sin and contentment is a grace learned through Christ.

title: Integrity and Uprightness
subtitle: Proverbs 11 — The Value of Righteousness
description: Proverbs 11 on the value of integrity, the fruit of righteousness as a tree of life, and the importance of wise counsel in the believer's walk.

title: The Way of the Righteous
subtitle: Proverbs 12 — Character in Daily Life
description: Proverbs 12 on the character of the righteous: loving correction, speaking truth, working diligently. Practical markers of a life shaped by wisdom.

title: Walking with God: The Puritan Daily Life
subtitle: A Devotional on Structuring Your Day
description: How the Puritans structured their entire day around devotion to God. Morning worship, family devotions, and evening examination of conscience from Richard Baxter.

title: The Fruit of Righteousness
subtitle: Proverbs 13 — Walking with the Wise
description: Proverbs 13 on hope deferred, the importance of discipline, and the transforming power of walking with wise companions. Key themes explored with pastoral warmth.

title: Spurgeon on the Sovereignty of Grace
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace in Spurgeon's Preaching
description: How Spurgeon preached the doctrines of grace: election, effectual calling, and perseverance. How sovereign grace simultaneously humbles pride and comforts the soul.

title: Wisdom Builds Her House
subtitle: Proverbs 14 — The Way That Seems Right
description: Proverbs 14 on the wise woman who builds her house, the fear of the Lord as a fountain of life, and the sobering warning about the way that seems right.

title: The Doctrine of Election
subtitle: From A.W. Pink's Studies in the Scriptures
description: From A.W. Pink's Studies in the Scriptures on the doctrine of election. What the Bible teaches about God's choosing, and why this produces humility, not pride.

title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
subtitle: Proverbs 15 — The Power of the Tongue
description: Proverbs 15 on the power of the tongue, the eyes of the Lord, and why a little with the fear of the Lord is better than great treasure with trouble.

title: The Lord Directs Our Steps
subtitle: Proverbs 16 — Surrendering Our Plans
description: Proverbs 16 on God working out everything to its proper end, pride before destruction, and the beauty of surrendering our plans to the Lord who directs our steps.

title: Justification by Faith Alone
subtitle: The Doctrine That Changes Everything
description: The Puritan understanding of justification by faith alone. How we are declared righteous before God through Christ. The doctrine that changes absolutely everything.

title: A Friend Loves at All Times
subtitle: Proverbs 17 — Friendship and Loyalty
description: Proverbs 17 on true friendship, covering offenses in love, and the healing power of a cheerful heart. With Spurgeon on Christian fellowship.

title: The Name of the Lord is a Strong Tower
subtitle: Proverbs 18 — Our Refuge in God
description: Proverbs 18:10 on finding security in God alone. The friend who sticks closer than a brother points to Christ. With A.W. Pink on the names of God.

title: The Whole Month in Review
subtitle: Looking Back on Our Journey Through Proverbs
description: A reflective look back over the entire month — from the fear of the Lord through wisdom, sin, grace, and justification. A benediction to carry forward.

title: The Foundation of Family Worship
subtitle: John Angell James — A Help to Domestic Happiness
memoryVerse: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might. -- Deuteronomy 6:5
discussionQuestions: What does God want families to talk about? (Hint: His words!)
When does God say we should talk about His truth — only at church, or all the time?
Why do you think God chose families, not just churches, as the main place to teach children about Him?
What are some practical ways we can 'write God's words on our doorposts' in our modern home?

title: Training Children in Godliness
subtitle: John Angell James — The Family Monitor
memoryVerse: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. -- Proverbs 22:6
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to 'train' someone? Is it the same as just telling them what to do?
Why do you think God says to start training children when they are young?
How is training a child like planting a seed and waiting for it to grow?
What is the difference between teaching someone rules and creating in them a love for what is right?

title: The Christian Home as a Little Church
subtitle: John Angell James — A Help to Domestic Happiness
description: The Christian Home as a Little Church
memoryVerse: But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. -- Joshua 24:15b
discussionQuestions: What did Joshua tell his family they would do? (Serve the Lord!)
What does it mean to call our home a 'little church'?
Why did Joshua say 'me and my house' instead of just 'me'? What does this teach us about family leadership?
How can we make sure our family worship is joyful and real, not just going through the motions?

title: The Power of Parental Example
subtitle: John Angell James — A Help to Domestic Happiness
memoryVerse: And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. -- Ephesians 6:4
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to 'provoke' someone? Can you think of a time someone made you really frustrated?
Why does the Bible say parents should not make their children angry?
Why do you think what people DO matters more than what they SAY?
How can parents show they are real and honest about their own faith, even when they make mistakes?

title: Reading Scripture Together
subtitle: John Angell James — A Help to Domestic Happiness
memoryVerse: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. -- Psalm 119:105
discussionQuestions: What does a lamp do? How is the Bible like a lamp for our lives?
What is your favorite story or verse in the Bible so far?
Why do you think the Psalmist said God's Word is sweeter than honey? Have you ever felt that way about Scripture?
How can we make our family Bible reading time more meaningful and enjoyable for everyone?

title: The Father's Sacred Calling
subtitle: John Angell James — The Family Monitor
memoryVerse: For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD. -- Genesis 18:19a
discussionQuestions: Who did God say would teach his children about the Lord? (Abraham!)
Why do you think God chose to tell Abraham His plans? What was special about Abraham as a father?
What does it mean to 'command' your household — is it about being bossy, or something deeper?
How can we encourage fathers (or father figures) in our lives to lead our families in knowing God?

title: The Mother's Gentle Influence
subtitle: John Angell James — A Help to Domestic Happiness
memoryVerse: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. -- Psalm 127:3
discussionQuestions: What does the Bible say children are? (A gift and reward from God!)
How are children like arrows? What does that picture teach us?
What is one thing your mother (or mother figure) has taught you about God?
Why do you think a mother's prayers are so powerful in a child's life?

title: Morning Devotion — Meeting God at Daybreak
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on the Psalms
description: Morning Devotion — Meeting God at Daybreak
memoryVerse: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up. -- Psalm 5:3
discussionQuestions: When does David talk to God — at night, in the afternoon, or in the morning?
Why do you think starting the day with prayer is better than waiting until bedtime?
What did Matthew Henry mean by calling the morning 'the gate of the day'?
What would our family mornings look like if we added a brief time of prayer before we start our day?

title: A Life of Prayer
subtitle: Matthew Henry — A Method for Prayer
memoryVerse: Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. -- 1 Thessalonians 5:17-18
discussionQuestions: Can you really pray ALL the time? What do you think that means?
What are some times during your regular day when you could talk to God?
What does it mean to give thanks 'in everything' — even hard things?
How can praying Scripture help us know what to say when we do not know how to pray?

title: New Mercies Every Morning
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on Lamentations
memoryVerse: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. -- Lamentations 3:22-23
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that God's mercies are 'new every morning'?
Jeremiah was very sad when he wrote this. Why is it amazing that he could still praise God?
Can you think of a time when God was faithful to your family even during a hard situation?
How does knowing God's mercies are new every morning help us face days that feel scary or overwhelming?

title: Trusting God in Trials
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on the Psalms
memoryVerse: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. -- Psalm 46:1
discussionQuestions: What is a refuge? Where do you go when you feel scared?
How is God like a strong fortress that keeps us safe?
Why does the psalmist say we do not need to fear even if the earth is shaken? What gives him that confidence?
Can you share a time when your family faced something hard and God helped you through it?

title: Loving Your Neighbor
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on Romans
memoryVerse: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another. -- Romans 12:10
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to be 'kindly affectioned' to someone?
What does 'in honour preferring one another' look like between brothers and sisters?
Why does Paul include so many different instructions in just a few verses? What picture does it paint?
How can our family be a 'fountain of love' that blesses others around us?

title: The Grace of Forgiveness
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on Colossians
memoryVerse: Even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. -- Colossians 3:13b
discussionQuestions: What does forgiveness mean? Is it easy or hard?
How many times did Jesus say we should forgive someone?
Why does Paul say we should forgive 'even as Christ forgave you'? How does knowing God forgave us help us forgive others?
What is the difference between forgiving someone and trusting them? Can you forgive someone and still set healthy boundaries?

title: The Lord's Day — A Gift of Rest and Worship
subtitle: Matthew Henry — Commentary on Isaiah
description: The Lord's Day — A Gift of Rest and Worship
memoryVerse: Call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable. -- Isaiah 58:13b
discussionQuestions: What does God call the Sabbath? (A delight!) Does that surprise you?
Why did God create a day of rest? Do you think we need it?
What is the difference between making the Lord's Day a burden and making it a delight?
What are some things our family could do to make our Lord's Day more restful, joyful, and God-centered?

title: What Makes a True Christian
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. -- Matthew 7:21
discussionQuestions: What does Jesus say about people who just say 'Lord, Lord' but do not obey God?
What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and actually knowing Him?
What did Secker mean when he said religion should be our nature, not just our garment?
How can we tell if our faith is real — not just going through the motions?

title: Walking the Talk
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. -- James 1:22
discussionQuestions: What happens when you look in a mirror and see something that needs fixing? Do you just walk away?
Why does James say hearing the Bible without obeying it is like forgetting what you saw in a mirror?
What does Secker mean by 'leaves without fruit'? Can you think of an example?
What is one thing we have learned from God's Word recently that we can put into action this week?

title: The Heart God Sees
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: For man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart. -- 1 Samuel 16:7b
discussionQuestions: Why did God choose David and not Eliab? What was different about them?
What does it mean that God looks at the heart? Can we fool God by looking good on the outside?
Why do you think people spend so much time on how they look on the outside instead of their hearts?
How does it make you feel to know that God sees the real you — and still loves you?

title: Unmasking Hypocrisy
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. -- Matthew 23:28
discussionQuestions: What is a 'whitewashed tomb'? Why did Jesus compare the Pharisees to one?
What does the word 'hypocrite' mean? (An actor who wears a mask!)
In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, why did God accept the tax collector's prayer?
How can we build a home where everyone feels safe to be honest and real instead of pretending?

title: Bearing Fruit for God's Glory
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. -- John 15:5
discussionQuestions: What happens to a branch that is cut off from a tree? Can it grow fruit on its own?
What does Jesus mean when He says 'abide in me'? How do we stay connected to Jesus?
What kind of 'fruit' does God want to grow in our lives? (Love, joy, peace, etc.)
Why does the gardener prune branches? How might God 'prune' things in our lives to help us grow?

title: The Narrow Way
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. -- Matthew 7:14
discussionQuestions: Jesus talks about two roads. What is different about them?
Why do you think more people choose the wide road?
What does it mean to enter the 'strait gate'? What do we have to leave behind?
How can our family help each other stay on the narrow way, especially when it gets hard?

title: Watching Your Words
subtitle: William Secker — The Nonsuch Professor
memoryVerse: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof. -- Proverbs 18:21
discussionQuestions: Can words really hurt people even though they are just words? Can you think of a time someone's words made you feel really good or really bad?
Why does James compare the tongue to a fire? How can a small thing cause big damage?
What does Jesus mean when He says 'out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh'?
What are some practical ways we can use our words to give life and encouragement in our family?

title: The Godly Person Prays
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
memoryVerse: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. -- Philippians 4:6
discussionQuestions: What does Paul say we should do instead of worrying?
What does it mean to pray 'in every thing'? Can you think of small things you could pray about?
Watson says prayer is like breathing for a Christian. What do you think he means?
What is the difference between praying because you have to and praying because you want to?

title: The Godly Person Loves God's Word
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
description: The Godly Person Loves God's Word
memoryVerse: O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. -- Psalm 119:97
discussionQuestions: The Psalmist says God's words are sweeter than honey. What is your favorite sweet treat? Can you imagine loving the Bible that much?
What is the difference between reading the Bible quickly and meditating on it?
Watson says the godly person treats the Bible like food, not medicine. What does that mean?
What is one way we could go deeper in our Bible reading as a family — not just reading more, but understanding more?

title: The Godly Person Lives by Faith
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
description: The Godly Person Lives by Faith
memoryVerse: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. -- Hebrews 11:1
discussionQuestions: Can you think of something you believe in even though you cannot see it? (Air, love, gravity?) How is faith like that?
Why does the Bible say it is impossible to please God without faith?
Which hero of faith from Hebrews 11 do you find most inspiring, and why?
Watson says even small, weak faith is accepted by God. How does that encourage you if your faith sometimes feels small?

title: The Godly Person Repents
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
memoryVerse: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. -- 1 John 1:9
discussionQuestions: What is the difference between being sorry you got caught and being truly sorry for what you did?
What does 'repentance' mean? Is it just saying sorry, or is it something more?
Why does God promise to forgive us when we confess? What makes Him willing to do that?
How can our family create a safe space where everyone can admit mistakes and receive grace?

title: The Godly Person Shows Charity
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
memoryVerse: My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. -- 1 John 3:18
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to love 'in deed and in truth' instead of just in words?
In the parable of the Good Samaritan, why do you think the priest and the Levite walked past the hurt man?
Jesus says that when we help someone in need, it is like helping Him. How does that change the way we think about serving others?
What is one way our family can show real, practical love to someone in need this week?

title: The Godly Person Pursues Holiness
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
memoryVerse: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. -- Hebrews 12:14
discussionQuestions: What does 'holy' mean? (Set apart for God!) Can you think of something that is set apart for a special purpose?
The Bible says 'without holiness no one will see the Lord.' Does that mean we have to be perfect? What does it mean?
Watson says the godly person is not sinless but cannot rest in sin. What is the difference between being perfect and always trying to grow?
What is one area of your life where you would like to grow in holiness? How can our family help each other?

title: The Godly Person Has Heavenly-Mindedness
subtitle: Thomas Watson — The Godly Man's Picture
memoryVerse: Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. -- Colossians 3:2
discussionQuestions: What does Paul mean when he says 'set your affection on things above'?
If heaven is our real home, how should that change the way we live right now?
Watson says the Christian uses the world like a traveler uses an inn. What does that picture mean to you?
What are some 'things above' that we should think about and value more? What are some 'things on earth' that we might value too much?

title: Using Time Wisely
subtitle: Richard Baxter — The Christian Directory
memoryVerse: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. -- Ephesians 5:15-16
discussionQuestions: What does 'redeeming the time' mean? How is time like a treasure?
What are some things that waste our time without us even realizing it?
How did Jesus use His time on earth? What can we learn from His example?
If you could add one hour to your day, how would you spend it? Does that answer reveal what you value most?

title: Contentment in All Circumstances
subtitle: Richard Baxter — The Christian Directory
memoryVerse: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. -- Philippians 4:11b
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to be content? Is it the same as not wanting anything?
Paul says he 'learned' to be content. Why is contentment something we have to learn?
What are some things that make us feel discontent? How can gratitude help?
How does trusting God make it easier to be content with what we have?

title: Preparing for Eternity
subtitle: Richard Baxter — The Christian Directory
memoryVerse: For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. -- 2 Corinthians 5:1
discussionQuestions: What does Paul say our bodies are like? (A tent!) What is the 'building from God' that is waiting for us?
What does heaven sound like based on Revelation 21:4? What are you most excited about?
Baxter says living with eternity in view helps us live well today. How does thinking about heaven change the way you face hard days?
As we finish this month of devotionals, what is the most important thing you have learned? How will you carry it forward?

title: Leaving the City of Destruction
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 1
memoryVerse: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat. -- Matthew 7:13
discussionQuestions: Why do you think most people choose the broad way instead of the narrow way?
Christian's family did not want to leave the City of Destruction. Have you ever felt alone in wanting to follow God?
What are some things in our world today that might be part of the 'City of Destruction' — things we need to turn away from?
What does it mean for our family to be on the narrow way together?

title: The Slough of Despond
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 2
memoryVerse: He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings. -- Psalm 40:2
discussionQuestions: Have you ever felt stuck in sadness or discouragement — like you were sinking in a swamp? What happened?
Why do you think Pliable went back to the City of Destruction instead of pushing through?
What are some of God's promises that can be 'stepping stones' when we feel discouraged?
How can our family be like the character Help — lifting each other up when someone is struggling?

title: The Wicket Gate
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 3
memoryVerse: I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. -- John 10:9
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that Jesus is the only door? Why can we not be saved any other way?
Christian knocked again and again at the gate. What does persistent knocking look like in our prayer life?
Arrows were being shot at Christian as he approached the gate. What kinds of 'arrows' does the enemy shoot at people who are seeking God?
Why must each person go through the gate for themselves? How can we help each other in our family come to know Jesus personally?

title: The Cross and the Burden
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 4
memoryVerse: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. -- Isaiah 53:5
discussionQuestions: Why could Christian not remove the burden himself? What does this teach us about trying to earn our own salvation?
What does it mean that Jesus bore our sins 'in his own body on the tree'?
Are you carrying any burdens of guilt or shame right now? How does looking at the cross help?
Why did the burden fall into a tomb? What is the connection between our sins and Jesus' burial?

title: The Hill Difficulty
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 5
memoryVerse: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. -- Hebrews 12:2
discussionQuestions: What is the hardest 'hill' your family has had to climb together? What did you learn from it?
Why did Formalist and Hypocrisy try to go around the hill? What 'shortcuts' do people try to take in their spiritual lives today?
How does looking at Jesus help us keep climbing when the way is steep and difficult?
James says to 'count it all joy' in trials. How can we find joy even when things are hard?

title: The Palace Beautiful
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 6
memoryVerse: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! -- Psalm 133:1
discussionQuestions: Why do you think God gave us the church? What would the Christian life be like without fellowship?
What are the 'lions' that keep people from being involved in a church? How do we overcome that fear?
How has our church family helped us grow as a family? Can you think of specific examples?
What does it mean to 'provoke one another to love and good works'? How can we do this for others?

title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 1, Day 7
description: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
memoryVerse: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. -- Psalm 23:4
discussionQuestions: What is the difference between a shadow and the real thing? Why is death called a 'shadow' for Christians?
Christian used 'All-prayer' when he could not use his sword. Why is prayer so important in our darkest moments?
Has our family ever gone through a 'dark valley'? How did God help us through it?
Isaiah 41:10 gives four promises. Which one do you need most right now?

title: What Is Contentment?
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 1
memoryVerse: But godliness with contentment is great gain. -- 1 Timothy 6:6
discussionQuestions: Paul said he 'learned' to be content. Why do you think contentment has to be learned rather than coming naturally?
What is the difference between contentment and laziness? Can you be content and still work hard?
What are some things our family tends to complain about? How might we view those things differently?
Burroughs calls contentment 'sweet.' Have you ever experienced a moment of genuine contentment? What was it like?

title: The Mystery of Contentment
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 2
memoryVerse: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. -- 2 Corinthians 12:9
discussionQuestions: What does Habakkuk's 'yet' teach us about faith? How can you say 'yet I will rejoice' when things go wrong?
Paul said God's strength is 'made perfect in weakness.' How have you seen God's strength show up most when you felt weakest?
Burroughs says contentment comes from subtracting desires, not adding possessions. What desires might our family need to subtract?
Why is the world's idea of happiness so different from biblical contentment?

title: Contentment vs. the World
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 3
memoryVerse: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. -- Matthew 6:21
discussionQuestions: John lists three categories of worldly temptation: lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and pride of life. Can you give examples of each from our everyday life?
What does Burroughs mean by the difference between a 'passage' and a 'portion'? How does seeing ourselves as pilgrims change our attitude toward things?
Jesus says moths, rust, and thieves destroy earthly treasures. What are some 'treasures' your family has seen fade or break?
What are some 'heavenly treasures' our family can store up together?

title: The Sin of Murmuring
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 4
memoryVerse: Do all things without murmurings and disputings. -- Philippians 2:14
discussionQuestions: Why was God so angry at the Israelites' complaining? What were they really saying about God when they murmured?
The Israelites remembered Egypt fondly even though it was a place of slavery. Do we ever romanticize things from our past that were not actually good for us?
How does complaining spread in a family? Can you think of times when one person's grumbling affected everyone?
What are three specific things you tend to complain about that you could replace with thanksgiving?

title: Contentment and Thankfulness
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 5
memoryVerse: In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. -- 1 Thessalonians 5:18
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul say 'in everything' rather than 'for everything'? What is the difference?
Psalm 100 says to 'know that the LORD he is God.' How does knowing who God is help us be thankful?
What are three specific things from today that you can thank God for right now?
How can our family build a daily habit of gratitude? What would that look like practically?

title: Contentment in Family Trials
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 6
memoryVerse: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. -- Romans 8:28
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that 'all things work together for good'? Does this mean everything that happens is good?
Job lost everything in a single day, yet he blessed God. What do you think gave him the strength to respond this way?
Can you think of a difficult time in our family's past that God used for good? How did He bring good out of it?
How can we help each other be content when one person in the family is going through a hard time?

title: The Secret of Seeking God First
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 2, Day 7
description: The Secret of Seeking God First
memoryVerse: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. -- Matthew 6:33
discussionQuestions: What does it mean practically for our family to 'seek first the kingdom of God'? What would change in our daily routine?
Psalm 37:4 says God gives us the desires of our heart when we delight in Him. How does delighting in God change what we desire?
Burroughs says God is an 'all-sufficient good.' What does it mean for God to be enough?
Looking back at this whole week on contentment, what is one thing our family wants to change or practice going forward?

title: Satan's Device: Making Sin Look Small
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 1
description: Satan's Device: Making Sin Look Small
memoryVerse: Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death. -- James 1:15
discussionQuestions: How did Satan make the forbidden fruit look appealing to Eve? What did he hide from her?
Can you think of ways our culture makes sin look small or harmless? Give some examples.
James describes a progression: desire, enticement, sin, death. Can you trace this pattern in a real-life example?
What does it mean to 'look at the hook, not just the bait' when it comes to temptation?

title: Satan's Device: Painting Sin with Virtue's Colors
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 2
description: Satan's Device: Painting Sin with Virtue's Colors
memoryVerse: Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness. -- Isaiah 5:20
discussionQuestions: Can you think of examples where our culture calls evil good or good evil?
Why is Satan described as an 'angel of light'? How does that make his deceptions more dangerous?
Brooks says Satan gives sins virtuous-sounding names. Can you think of a sin that has been renamed to sound acceptable?
How can studying God's Word help us see through Satan's disguises?

title: Satan's Device: The Secrecy of Sin
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 3
description: Satan's Device: The Secrecy of Sin
memoryVerse: Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. -- Hebrews 4:13
discussionQuestions: Why does Satan want us to think secret sin is safe? What makes hidden sin more dangerous than open sin?
What does it mean that 'your sin will find you out'? Can you think of examples from the Bible or from life?
How does knowing that God sees everything make you feel? Is it frightening or comforting — or both?
How can our family create a safe environment where we can be honest about our struggles?

title: Remedy: Keep Eternity in View
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 4
memoryVerse: While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal. -- 2 Corinthians 4:18
discussionQuestions: How does thinking about eternity change the way we look at our problems today?
Paul called his severe sufferings 'light' and 'momentary.' What made him able to see them that way?
How does keeping eternity in view help us resist temptation? Can you give a specific example?
What excites you most about eternity with God?

title: Remedy: Flee Temptation
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 5
memoryVerse: Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart. -- 2 Timothy 2:22
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul say 'flee' rather than 'fight' when it comes to certain temptations? When is running the best strategy?
God promises a 'way of escape' with every temptation. Can you think of a time when you saw that escape route?
What does Brooks mean by 'dancing on the brink'? How do people get too close to temptation in everyday life?
What practical 'escape routes' can our family set up for the temptations we face most?

title: Remedy: Stay in God's Word
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 6
memoryVerse: Thy word have I hid in my heart, that I might not sin against thee. -- Psalm 119:11
discussionQuestions: How did Jesus use Scripture to defeat Satan in the wilderness? What does this teach us about the power of God's Word?
What does it mean to 'hide' God's Word in your heart? How is this different from just reading the Bible?
Why is Scripture called 'the sword of the Spirit'? What makes it an offensive weapon?
What verse would you most want to have ready when temptation comes? Why?

title: Remedy: Pray Without Ceasing
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 3, Day 7
memoryVerse: Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. -- Matthew 26:41
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to 'pray without ceasing'? How can we pray all the time while also doing our daily work?
Jesus told the disciples to 'watch and pray.' What happened when they slept instead? What lesson is there for us?
Why should prayer be our first response to temptation rather than our last resort?
What is one change our family can make this week to strengthen our prayer life together?

title: Christ Is Altogether Lovely
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 1
memoryVerse: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord. -- Philippians 3:8
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that Christ is 'altogether lovely'? Can you name specific things about Jesus that are beautiful to you?
Paul gave up everything for Jesus and called it all 'dung.' What would it look like for our family to value Jesus above everything else?
Rutherford said he saw more of Christ in exile than ever before. Why do we often see Jesus more clearly during hard times?
What is the difference between serving Jesus out of duty and serving Him out of love? Which describes our family more?

title: Suffering Produces Glory
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 2
memoryVerse: For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. -- Romans 8:18
discussionQuestions: How is suffering like 'wings on a bird' or 'sails on a ship,' as Rutherford described?
Paul says affliction 'worketh for us' glory. Can you think of a time when something hard in your life produced something good?
What is the difference between God punishing us and God refining us? How does knowing Jesus changes the meaning of suffering?
How can our family encourage each other when someone is going through a hard time?

title: The Sweetness of Christ in Trials
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 3
description: The Sweetness of Christ in Trials
memoryVerse: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. -- 1 Peter 1:8
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to 'taste and see' that the Lord is good? How is tasting different from just knowing?
Peter says trial of faith is more precious than gold. Why would a tested faith be more valuable than wealth?
Rutherford found more sweetness in Christ during exile than during comfort. Why might that be true?
Can you share a time when you experienced God's goodness during a difficult period?

title: Waiting on the Lord
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 4
memoryVerse: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. -- Isaiah 40:31
discussionQuestions: Why is waiting so hard? What does our difficulty with waiting reveal about our hearts?
Isaiah mentions mounting up, running, and walking. Which one do you think is hardest? Why does walking without fainting require the most strength?
Can you think of a time our family had to wait for something and God came through?
What is our family currently waiting for? How can we wait well together?

title: The Love of Christ Constrains Us
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 5
description: The Love of Christ Constrains Us
memoryVerse: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. -- Romans 8:38-39
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that Christ's love 'constrains' us? How does His love change the way we live?
Paul lists many things that cannot separate us from God's love. Which one is most meaningful to you tonight?
How should the unbreakable love of Christ affect the way we love each other in our family?
Rutherford compared Christ's love to an ocean. What other images come to mind when you think about how big God's love is?

title: Heaven Is Our Home
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 6
memoryVerse: In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. -- John 14:2
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that our citizenship is in heaven? How should that change the way we live on earth?
Jesus said He is preparing a place for us. What do you imagine that place will be like?
What is the greatest thing about heaven — the place, the people, or the presence of Jesus?
How does thinking about heaven help us face the hard things in this life?

title: Christ's Crown and Covenant
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Week 4, Day 7
memoryVerse: Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. -- Revelation 2:10
discussionQuestions: What does it mean to be 'faithful unto death'? Does this mean we have to be perfect?
Paul said the crown is for 'all them that love his appearing.' Do you love the thought of Jesus returning? Why or why not?
Rutherford was summoned before Parliament but said he had a higher summons. What does this teach us about our ultimate allegiance?
Looking back at this week with Rutherford, what has been the most meaningful lesson for you?

title: Looking Back at Our Pilgrimage
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Synthesis, Day 1
memoryVerse: I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. -- Psalm 77:11
discussionQuestions: Looking back at this month, which week's theme was most meaningful to your family? Why?
Can you share one specific thing God taught you through these devotionals?
Why does God command us to remember? How does looking back strengthen our faith for the future?
What is one practice from this month that you want to continue as a family going forward?

title: Looking Forward in Faith
subtitle: Pilgrim Families — Synthesis, Day 2
memoryVerse: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. -- Philippians 1:6
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that God will 'perform' (complete) the good work He began in us? How is this different from us completing it ourselves?
Jude says God will present us 'faultless' before His glory. How is this possible for people who still sin every day?
Bunyan wrote, 'All the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.' What does this image mean to you?
As we look ahead as a family, what is one commitment we want to make for the next month of our pilgrimage together?

title: God's Holiness & Our Reverence
subtitle: Knowing God — His Attributes
reviewQuestions: In what year and under what circumstances did Isaiah receive his vision of God's holiness?
How many wings did each seraphim have, and what was the purpose of each pair?
What is the significance of the threefold repetition of 'Holy' in Isaiah 6:3?
What was Isaiah's immediate response when he saw the holiness of God?
How was Isaiah's sin purged, and what does this prefigure about Christ's work?
activity: Students will create an illuminated manuscript page of Isaiah 6:1-7. Using calligraphy pens or fine-tipped markers on parchment-style paper, students will carefully copy the full text of Isaiah 6:1-7 in their best handwriting. Around the margins, they will illustrate the key elements of the vision: the throne, the seraphims with six wings, the live coal, and the smoke filling the temple. Each illustration should include a brief annotation explaining its theological significance (e.g., 'Wings covering face = even sinless angels cannot gaze upon God's full holiness'). Students should use gold or yellow coloring for the throne and divine glory, red for the coal from the altar, and leave white space around the threefold 'Holy' to emphasize its centrality. This exercise combines artistic expression with careful meditation on the text.

title: God's Sovereignty & Our Trust
subtitle: Knowing God — His Attributes
reviewQuestions: What did Nebuchadnezzar declare about God's sovereignty after his reason was restored in Daniel 4:35?
What analogy does Paul use in Romans 9:19-21 to illustrate God's sovereign authority?
According to Isaiah 46:9-10, how does God's sovereignty relate to His knowledge of the future?
How did Watson explain the relationship between God's sovereignty and the practice of prayer?
What is the difference between God's decretive will and His preceptive will, as Charnock explained it?
activity: Students will create a 'Sovereignty Timeline' tracing how God's sovereign hand directed events in the life of Joseph (Genesis 37-50). On a large sheet of poster paper, students will draw a horizontal timeline and mark each major event: Joseph's dreams, his brothers' jealousy, being sold into slavery, Potiphar's house, false accusation, prison, interpreting dreams, rise to power, famine, brothers' arrival in Egypt, and the family reunion. For each event, students must write two entries: (1) what it looked like from a human perspective (often painful or unjust), and (2) what God was accomplishing through it from a sovereign perspective. The timeline should visually show how God wove even sinful human actions into His perfect plan, culminating in Joseph's declaration in Genesis 50:20.

title: God's Love & Our Gratitude
subtitle: Knowing God — His Attributes
reviewQuestions: What does John mean when he says 'God is love' in 1 John 4:8?
According to 1 John 4:10, how was God's love manifested toward us?
What does the word 'propitiation' mean and why is it important?
According to Jeremiah 31:3, what is the nature and duration of God's love?
How did Charnock distinguish between God's general love and His special saving love?
activity: Students will write a personal essay titled 'The Love That Would Not Let Me Go.' Using the biblical texts studied in this lesson as their foundation, students will compose a 500-word essay exploring what God's love means to them personally. The essay must include at least three direct Scripture quotations, a reference to either Charnock or Watson's teaching on divine love, and a specific application of how understanding God's love should change the way they treat others. Students should structure their essay with an introduction, three body paragraphs (the nature of God's love, the proof of God's love at the cross, and the application of God's love in daily life), and a conclusion. Encourage students to write from the heart while maintaining theological accuracy.

title: God's Justice & Our Obedience
subtitle: Knowing God — His Attributes
reviewQuestions: According to Deuteronomy 32:4, in what ways is God described as perfectly just?
What does Romans 3:25-26 tell us about why God set forth Christ as a propitiation?
What does Nahum 1:3 mean when it says God 'will not at all acquit the wicked'?
What is the difference between remunerative justice and punitive justice as Watson explained them?
How did the Puritans explain the relationship between God's justice and God's mercy at the cross?
activity: Students will conduct a 'Justice and Mercy at the Cross' analysis. Working individually or in small groups, students will create a two-column chart on poster paper. The left column is titled 'The Demands of Justice' and the right column 'The Provision of Mercy.' Students will look up and write out key Scripture passages that describe each: passages about the penalty of sin, the wrath of God, and the necessity of punishment on the justice side; passages about God's love, Christ's sacrifice, and the offer of forgiveness on the mercy side. In the center between the two columns, students will draw or describe the cross, showing how it is the meeting point where justice and mercy converge. Each group will present their chart to the class, explaining how the cross satisfies both attributes simultaneously.

title: God's Faithfulness & Our Hope
subtitle: Knowing God — His Attributes
reviewQuestions: What is the historical context of Lamentations 3:22-23, and why does this context make the declaration of God's faithfulness so remarkable?
What does Deuteronomy 7:9 tell us about the duration and nature of God's faithfulness?
According to 2 Timothy 2:13, what happens to God's faithfulness when believers are unfaithful?
How did Charnock connect God's immutability to His faithfulness?
What did Watson mean when he said that God sometimes shows His faithfulness by afflicting His people?
activity: Students will create a 'Faithfulness Journal' by looking through the Old Testament and documenting at least ten specific promises God made and how He fulfilled them. For each entry, students should record: (1) the promise God made, with the Scripture reference; (2) the person or people to whom it was given; (3) the circumstances in which it was given; (4) how and when God fulfilled it, with the Scripture reference; and (5) what this teaches us about God's character. Students should present their journals to the class and discuss patterns they observe — such as God's timing, the way He fulfills promises in unexpected ways, and His faithfulness even when His people are unfaithful. The journal can be handwritten and illustrated or typed and printed.

title: Starting the Journey — Conviction & Conversion
subtitle: The Pilgrim's Journey
reviewQuestions: What does the word 'pricked' mean in Acts 2:37, and what caused this reaction in Peter's audience?
What two things did Peter command his hearers to do in Acts 2:38?
What does Ezekiel 36:26 promise that God will do in the hearts of His people?
In Pilgrim's Progress, what does Christian's burden represent, and where does it finally fall off?
Why did Bunyan include characters like Formalist and Talkative in his allegory?
activity: Students will create a detailed map of the first portion of Christian's journey in 'The Pilgrim's Progress,' from the City of Destruction to the cross. Using a large sheet of poster paper, students should illustrate and label each location: the City of Destruction, the Slough of Despond, the Wicket Gate, the Interpreter's House, the Hill of Difficulty, and the Cross. At each location, students should write a brief description of what happens there and the biblical truth it represents. For example, at the Slough of Despond, students would write about the doubts and fears that assail seeking sinners and reference relevant Scriptures. The map should include paths, terrain features, and key characters encountered along the way. This visual exercise helps students internalize Bunyan's allegorical method and connect his imagery to biblical doctrine.

title: The Valley of Humiliation — Suffering Well
subtitle: The Pilgrim's Journey
description: The Valley of Humiliation — Suffering Well
reviewQuestions: What does James 1:2-4 say is the result of the 'trying of faith'?
What is the chain of spiritual growth described in Romans 5:3-5?
In Pilgrim's Progress, what three strategies does Apollyon use against Christian in the Valley of Humiliation?
How does Christian defeat Apollyon, and what does this represent spiritually?
What four purposes of suffering did the Puritans identify from Scripture?
activity: Students will write a reflective essay titled 'My Valley of Humiliation.' Drawing from the biblical teaching and Bunyan's allegory, students will reflect on a time of difficulty or trial in their own lives (or in the life of a biblical character they identify with) and analyze it through the lens of this lesson. The essay should address: (1) What was the nature of the trial? (2) How did it feel at the time? (3) What spiritual attacks or temptations accompanied it? (4) How did God's Word and God's presence sustain you (or the biblical character) through it? (5) What spiritual fruit came from the experience? Students should reference at least two Scripture passages and one insight from Bunyan or the Puritans. This is a personal and devotional exercise, so students should write honestly and reflectively.

title: Vanity Fair — Living in the World
subtitle: The Pilgrim's Journey
description: Vanity Fair — Living in the World
reviewQuestions: What three categories of worldly temptation does John identify in 1 John 2:15-17?
What does Romans 12:1-2 say is the alternative to being conformed to the world?
In Pilgrim's Progress, what happens to Christian and Faithful when they refuse to buy anything at Vanity Fair?
What was the fate of Faithful at Vanity Fair, and what does it represent spiritually?
What balanced approach to the world did the Puritans advocate — neither asceticism nor worldliness?
activity: Students will create a modern-day 'Vanity Fair Marketplace.' On a large poster or whiteboard, students will design a market layout with booths representing the things the modern world offers as substitutes for God: entertainment, social media fame, material wealth, romantic relationships apart from God's design, academic prestige, physical appearance, and others. For each booth, students should write: (1) what the world promises this will provide, (2) what it actually delivers in the long run, and (3) what biblical truth exposes the emptiness of this false promise. At the center of the marketplace, students should place a sign pointing to the narrow gate that leads out of Vanity Fair, with a relevant Scripture verse. This exercise helps students critically evaluate the worldly values that surround them daily.

title: Doubting Castle — Overcoming Doubt
subtitle: The Pilgrim's Journey
reviewQuestions: What was the father's prayer in Mark 9:24, and what does it teach us about the nature of faith?
How does Hebrews 11:1 define faith, and why is this definition important for combating doubt?
In Pilgrim's Progress, how did Christian and Hopeful end up in Doubting Castle?
What was the 'key of Promise' that opened the doors of Doubting Castle, and what does it represent?
What distinction did the Puritans make between doubt and unbelief?
activity: Students will create a 'Key of Promise' booklet. Using cardstock cut into the shape of an old-fashioned key, students will create a small booklet where each page contains one promise of God that can unlock the dungeon of doubt. Students should find and write out at least ten promises from Scripture, covering various types of doubt: doubt about salvation (John 10:28-29), doubt about forgiveness (1 John 1:9), doubt about God's love (Romans 8:38-39), doubt about God's presence (Hebrews 13:5), doubt about the future (Jeremiah 29:11), doubt about provision (Philippians 4:19), and others. Each page should include the full verse in KJV, a one-sentence summary of the promise, and a brief note about when this promise would be especially helpful. This booklet becomes a practical tool students can carry with them.

title: The Celestial City — Persevering to the End
subtitle: The Pilgrim's Journey
description: The Celestial City — Persevering to the End
reviewQuestions: What three metaphors does Paul use in 2 Timothy 4:7 to describe his life of faithfulness?
According to Hebrews 12:1-2, what three things should Christians do to run the race of faith?
In Pilgrim's Progress, what obstacle lies between the land of Beulah and the Celestial City?
What happened to the character Ignorance at the gate of the Celestial City, and what does it teach?
How did the Puritans understand the doctrine of 'perseverance of the saints'?
activity: Students will create a comprehensive 'Pilgrim's Progress Journey Map' that covers the entire allegory from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City. Using a large sheet of butcher paper (at least 4 feet long), students will map Christian's complete journey, marking and illustrating every major location, character, and event. Each location should include a brief description and the biblical truth it represents. Students should use different colors to indicate different types of experiences: green for places of spiritual growth, red for places of danger and temptation, blue for places of refreshment and comfort, and gold for the final destination. This project synthesizes all five lessons on Bunyan's allegory and produces a visual reference that students can keep.

title: Christ as Prophet — Learning from Him
subtitle: The Work of Christ
description: Christ as Prophet — Learning from Him
reviewQuestions: What prophecy in Deuteronomy 18:15 did Christ fulfill as the great Prophet?
According to John 1:14-18, what unique qualification does Christ have as the revealer of God?
How did the crowds respond to Jesus' teaching in Matthew 7:28-29, and why?
What three dimensions of Christ's prophetic ministry were identified in the lesson?
How did Flavel explain the difference between Christ's external teaching through the Word and His internal teaching through the Spirit?
activity: Students will conduct a comparative study of Christ's prophetic teaching in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7). Working in small groups, each group will be assigned one section of the Sermon: the Beatitudes (5:1-12), salt and light (5:13-16), the law fulfilled (5:17-48), prayer and fasting (6:1-18), treasures and anxiety (6:19-34), or judging and the two ways (7:1-29). Each group will prepare a presentation that includes: (1) a summary of what Christ teaches in their section, (2) how this teaching demonstrates His prophetic authority (noting where He says 'I say unto you'), (3) how this teaching reveals the character and will of God, and (4) a practical application for daily life. Groups will present their findings to the class, building a comprehensive picture of Christ the Prophet at work.

title: Christ as Priest — His Sacrifice for Us
subtitle: The Work of Christ
description: Christ as Priest — His Sacrifice for Us
reviewQuestions: What does the phrase 'to the uttermost' in Hebrews 7:25 mean?
What five qualities describe Christ as High Priest in Hebrews 7:26?
How does Hebrews 9:11-14 contrast Christ's sacrifice with the Old Testament animal sacrifices?
What does Isaiah 53:5-6 teach about the substitutionary nature of Christ's death?
How did Flavel describe the sufficiency of Christ's blood for even the greatest sins?
activity: Students will create a detailed comparison chart showing the parallels between the Old Testament sacrificial system and the sacrifice of Christ. Using a large sheet of paper divided into columns, students will compare: (1) the Passover Lamb with Christ as 'our Passover' (1 Corinthians 5:7), (2) the Day of Atonement offerings with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 9-10), (3) the daily burnt offerings with the continual efficacy of Christ's blood, (4) the qualifications of Old Testament priests with the qualifications of Christ as High Priest (Hebrews 7:26), and (5) the earthly tabernacle with the heavenly sanctuary Christ entered. For each comparison, students should note both the similarities and the ways in which Christ's priesthood far surpasses the Old Testament system.

title: Christ as King — His Rule in Our Lives
subtitle: The Work of Christ
description: Christ as King — His Rule in Our Lives
reviewQuestions: What does Philippians 2:9-11 say about the ultimate extent of Christ's kingship?
According to Psalm 2:6-8, who appointed Christ as King and what was given to Him?
What two aspects of Christ's kingship were distinguished in the lesson?
What three aspects of Christ's kingly work did Flavel identify?
How did the Puritans understand the relationship between Christ's spiritual kingdom and earthly institutions?
activity: Students will write a declaration of allegiance to Christ the King. Modeled on historic declarations and covenants (such as the Scottish National Covenant or the Puritan church covenants), students will compose a formal, thoughtful written statement declaring their submission to the lordship of Christ over specific areas of their lives. The declaration should include: (1) an acknowledgment of who Christ is (His qualifications as King), (2) specific areas of life they are placing under His authority (academics, relationships, entertainment, future plans, thought life), (3) a commitment to obey His Word as their supreme rule of life, and (4) a reliance on His grace for the strength to fulfill this commitment. Students should write seriously and reverently, as this is a spiritual exercise, not merely an academic one.

title: Union with Christ — Living in Him
subtitle: The Work of Christ
description: Union with Christ — Living in Him
reviewQuestions: In John 15:1-7, what does the vine represent, what do the branches represent, and what does the Father do as the husbandman?
What does Galatians 2:20 teach about the believer's union with Christ in His death and resurrection?
According to Ephesians 2:4-6, what three things have happened to believers because of their union with Christ?
How did Flavel describe union with Christ as the foundation of all other spiritual blessings?
What three analogies did Flavel use to illustrate union with Christ, and what does each emphasize?
activity: Students will create a visual diagram illustrating the doctrine of union with Christ. Using a large vine and branches drawing as the central image, students will show how each spiritual blessing flows from union with Christ. The vine trunk represents Christ; the branches represent individual believers; the roots represent the Holy Spirit who unites us to Christ; and the fruit represents the spiritual benefits that flow from this union. Students should label specific fruits with their corresponding blessings: justification, sanctification, adoption, peace with God, access to prayer, spiritual power, hope of glory, and others. Around the margin, students should write key Scripture references for each blessing. This visual theology exercise helps students see the centrality and comprehensiveness of union with Christ.

title: The Fountain of Life — Daily Dependence
subtitle: The Work of Christ
description: The Fountain of Life — Daily Dependence
reviewQuestions: In John 4:13-14, how does Jesus contrast the water from Jacob's well with the water He gives?
What does Psalm 36:9 mean when it says 'with thee is the fountain of life'?
According to Revelation 22:1-2, what flows from the throne of God in the eternal city?
What four services of a fountain did Flavel identify as illustrations of Christ's work?
How did Flavel address believers who felt too unworthy to come to the fountain of Christ?
activity: Students will create a comprehensive 'Fountain of Life' study guide that synthesizes all five lessons on the work of Christ. The study guide should include: (1) a section on Christ as Prophet with key Scriptures and Flavel's insights, (2) a section on Christ as Priest with the comparison chart from Lesson 12, (3) a section on Christ as King with the implications for daily life, (4) a section on Union with Christ with the vine and branches imagery, and (5) a section on the Fountain of Life with the four services of the fountain. Each section should include memory verses, key definitions, and personal application points. This study guide serves as a review of the entire unit and as a resource students can keep for future reference.

title: The Belt of Truth — Honesty & Integrity
subtitle: Spiritual Armor
description: The Belt of Truth — Honesty & Integrity
reviewQuestions: What was the function of the belt in a Roman soldier's equipment, and why is truth compared to it?
What three dimensions of truth were identified in the lesson?
According to John 8:44, what is the fundamental character of Satan, and how does this relate to the belt of truth?
What three aspects of truth did Gurnall identify in his exposition of Ephesians 6:14a?
How did Gurnall warn that Satan uses Scripture itself as a tool of deception?
activity: Students will conduct a 'Truth Audit' of their daily lives. Using a prepared worksheet, students will honestly evaluate the role of truth in several areas of their lives: (1) Doctrinal knowledge — How well do I know the fundamental doctrines of the Christian faith? (2) Scripture engagement — How regularly do I read and study God's Word? (3) Personal honesty — Am I truthful in my speech, or do I exaggerate, deceive, or present a false image? (4) Intellectual integrity — Am I willing to follow the truth wherever it leads, even when it is uncomfortable? (5) Worship — Is my worship genuine, or am I going through the motions? Students will write honest, private reflections on each area and identify one specific action they can take to strengthen the belt of truth in their lives.

title: The Breastplate of Righteousness — Right Living
subtitle: Spiritual Armor
description: The Breastplate of Righteousness — Right Living
reviewQuestions: What was the function of the breastplate in Roman armor, and what spiritual reality does it represent?
What is the difference between imputed righteousness and practical righteousness?
According to Isaiah 61:10 and Philippians 3:9, where does the believer's foundational righteousness come from?
How did Gurnall counsel believers who were struggling with guilt and condemnation?
What did Gurnall identify as common areas where Christians remove their breastplate through unrighteousness?
activity: Students will create a two-sided visual representation of the breastplate of righteousness. On one side (labeled 'Imputed Righteousness'), students will write out key Scriptures about the righteousness of Christ credited to believers through faith, including Romans 3:21-22, Isaiah 61:10, Philippians 3:9, and 2 Corinthians 5:21. On the other side (labeled 'Practical Righteousness'), students will list specific areas of daily life where righteous conduct serves as spiritual protection, with corresponding Scriptures and practical applications. Students should decorate the breastplate shape with relevant symbols and images and include a Gurnall quote on each side. This exercise reinforces the complementary nature of both aspects of righteousness.

title: The Shield of Faith — Standing Firm
subtitle: Spiritual Armor
description: The Shield of Faith — Standing Firm
reviewQuestions: What was the Roman 'thureos' shield, and why was it soaked in water before battle?
According to Hebrews 11:1, what is faith?
What does 1 John 5:4 say about the relationship between faith and victory?
What five types of fiery darts did Gurnall identify?
How did Gurnall explain the relationship between the strength of faith and the object of faith?
activity: Students will create a 'Shield of Faith' study card system. Using index cards, students will write one biblical promise on each card and organize them by category: promises for temptation, promises for accusation/guilt, promises for doubt, promises for fear, and promises for discouragement. Each card should have the full KJV text of the promise on one side and a brief explanation of how to apply it during spiritual attack on the other. Students should create at least fifteen cards (three per category) and bind them together with a ring or keep them in a small pouch. This portable 'shield' can be carried and consulted whenever a specific spiritual attack occurs, providing immediate, Scripture-based defense.

title: The Sword of the Spirit — God's Word
subtitle: Spiritual Armor
description: The Sword of the Spirit — God's Word
reviewQuestions: Why is the sword of the Spirit unique among the pieces of spiritual armor?
How did Jesus use the Word of God against Satan in the wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:1-11)?
According to 2 Timothy 3:16-17, what are the four purposes for which Scripture is profitable?
What three ways of using the sword of the Spirit did Gurnall identify?
Why did Gurnall insist that the Word of God must be accompanied by the power of the Holy Spirit?
activity: Students will engage in a 'Sword Drill' competition, but with a spiritual warfare twist. Rather than simply finding verses quickly, students will be given scenarios describing specific spiritual attacks (temptation to lie, feelings of condemnation, fear of the future, doubt about God's love, pressure to conform to the world). For each scenario, students must find and read aloud an appropriate Scripture passage that directly addresses the attack — just as Jesus used specific texts against specific temptations. Students earn points not only for speed but for the accuracy and relevance of their chosen passage. This exercise develops the practical skill of matching biblical promises and truths to specific spiritual challenges.

title: The Helmet of Salvation — Confident Hope
subtitle: Spiritual Armor
description: The Helmet of Salvation — Confident Hope
reviewQuestions: What did the helmet protect in Roman warfare, and what does the helmet of salvation protect spiritually?
How does 1 Thessalonians 5:8 clarify the meaning of the helmet of salvation?
What are the three tenses of salvation (past, present, future), and how do they relate to the helmet?
What three grounds of assurance did Gurnall identify?
How did Gurnall envision the day when the spiritual armor would be exchanged for a crown?
activity: Students will create a comprehensive 'Spiritual Armor Review' that synthesizes all five lessons on the armor of God. Using a full-sized outline of a human figure drawn on butcher paper, students will draw and label each piece of armor in its proper position: belt (truth), breastplate (righteousness), shoes (gospel of peace — mentioned in passing as context), shield (faith), helmet (salvation), and sword (Word of God). For each piece, students should write: (1) the spiritual reality it represents, (2) the key Scripture verse, (3) one insight from William Gurnall, and (4) one practical application for daily life. This completed figure should be displayed as a reminder of the resources God provides for spiritual warfare.

title: Total Depravity — Our Great Need
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
unit: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
reviewQuestions: Define total depravity in your own words. What does 'total' mean in this context?
According to Romans 3:10-18, what are the specific effects of sin on human speech, actions, and attitudes?
What does Paul mean in Ephesians 2:1 when he says we were 'dead in trespasses and sins'?
How does the Westminster Confession Chapter 6 describe the effects of Adam's fall on all his posterity?
According to Thomas Boston, why can the fallen will not choose spiritual good?
activity: Students will create a 'Fourfold State' diagram based on Thomas Boston's framework. On a large sheet of poster paper divided into four quadrants, students will illustrate the four states of human nature: (1) Innocence — Adam and Eve in the Garden, with the faculties of mind, will, and affections all properly ordered toward God; (2) Nature — the fall and its effects, with arrows showing how each faculty has been corrupted; (3) Grace — the work of regeneration, with Scripture verses showing how God restores each corrupted faculty; (4) Glory — the final state, where every faculty is perfected. For each quadrant, students should include at least two Scripture references and one quote from Boston or the Westminster Confession. The visual should clearly show the contrast between the devastation of the fall and the restoration of grace.

title: Unconditional Election — God's Sovereign Choice
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
unit: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
reviewQuestions: What does 'unconditional' mean in the phrase 'unconditional election'?
According to Ephesians 1:4-6, when did God choose His people, and on what basis?
What does Romans 9:16 teach about the ultimate cause of salvation?
How did John Owen respond to the Arminian claim that God elects based on foreseen faith?
What is the purpose of election according to Ephesians 1:4, and how does this refute the charge that election leads to sinful living?
activity: Students will conduct a 'Scripture chain' study of election by creating a visual chain of linked paper strips, each containing a key verse about God's sovereign choice. Starting with Ephesians 1:4, students will trace the doctrine of election through at least 12 passages across both Testaments (including Deuteronomy 7:7-8, Psalm 65:4, Isaiah 43:1, John 6:37, 6:44, 10:16, 15:16, 17:9, Acts 13:48, Romans 8:29-30, 9:11-16, 2 Thessalonians 2:13). Each link should contain the verse reference on one side and a brief summary of what it teaches about election on the other. When completed, students will display their chain and explain how the passages build upon one another to present a unified biblical doctrine.

title: Limited Atonement — Christ's Particular Redemption
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
unit: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
reviewQuestions: What is a more accurate name for 'limited atonement,' and why is it preferred?
In John 10:11-15, for whom does Jesus say He lays down His life? What does this imply about the scope of the atonement?
Summarize John Owen's trilemma argument from 'The Death of Death in the Death of Christ.'
How does Isaiah 53:10-11 support the doctrine of particular redemption, especially the phrase 'he shall see his seed'?
What is the difference between the sufficiency and the efficiency of Christ's death?
activity: Students will engage in a structured debate on the extent of the atonement. The class will be divided into two teams: one representing the particular redemption position and the other representing the general atonement position. Each team will be given 30 minutes to prepare their case using Scripture references, logical arguments, and quotations from theologians. The debate will follow a formal structure: opening statements (3 minutes each), direct examination of key texts (10 minutes), cross-examination (5 minutes each), and closing arguments (3 minutes each). After the debate, the class will evaluate which position best accounts for ALL the biblical evidence. The teacher should guide students to see how particular redemption fits within the broader framework of the doctrines of grace.

title: Irresistible Grace — The Effectual Call
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
unit: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
reviewQuestions: What does 'irresistible grace' mean, and how is it different from the idea that God forces people to believe against their will?
According to John 6:44, what is required before any person can come to Christ?
How does Ezekiel 36:26-27 describe God's work in changing the human heart?
What distinction did Thomas Goodwin draw between the outward call and the inward, effectual call?
According to the Westminster Confession Chapter 10, in what sense do the elect come to Christ 'most freely'?
activity: Students will study and compare three biblical conversion narratives: Paul (Acts 9:1-19), Lydia (Acts 16:13-15), and the Philippian jailer (Acts 16:25-34). For each account, students will create a detailed analysis chart with the following categories: (1) the person's spiritual condition before conversion, (2) the circumstances through which God worked, (3) evidence of the outward call (human instrumentality), (4) evidence of the inward call (divine initiative), (5) the immediate response, and (6) the fruits of conversion. Students will then write a one-page reflection comparing the three accounts and identifying the common elements of effectual calling present in each, noting how the sovereign work of God adapts to different personalities and circumstances while always producing the same essential result: faith and repentance.

title: Perseverance of the Saints — Kept by God
subtitle: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
description: Perseverance of the Saints — Kept by God
unit: The Doctrines of Grace — Westminster Standards
reviewQuestions: What does the doctrine of perseverance of the saints teach, and on what does it ultimately depend?
According to John 10:27-29, what three assurances does Jesus give His sheep regarding their eternal security?
What is the 'golden chain' of Romans 8:29-30, and why does it guarantee that all the elect will be glorified?
How does Jeremiah 32:40 show that God secures both His own faithfulness and His people's faithfulness within the covenant of grace?
According to Owen, how should the doctrine of perseverance motivate holiness rather than carelessness?
